tagline: Down off the flat horizon into a glacier's trench.
intro: From Baldhill Dam, where the Sheyenne backs up into Lake Ashtabula, the byway heads south and drops into a valley that eastern North Dakota keeps out of sight. Meltwater from the Wisconsin glacier cut it about 13,000 years ago. It runs up to 330 feet deep and a mile wide, and the flat horizon stays up on the rim.

Below, the road follows the river through Valley City and its bridges, then on by Kathryn and Fort Ransom to Lisbon, 63 miles in all. From Highway 46 down to Fort Ransom it began as an Indian footpath, and a settler named Amos Olson is credited with clearing most of the road between Preston and Fort Ransom.
season: Fall. Midwest Living magazine suggests the road as a fall color drive.

moments.title: Hi-Line Railroad Bridge
moments.text: The Northern Pacific finished it in 1908 to skip the steep grades in and out of the valley, 3,860 feet long and 162 feet over the river, and freight trains still cross.

moments.title: Fort Ransom
moments.text: In 1972 the Fort Ransom Commercial Club put a Viking statue on Pyramid Hill. Geologists call the hill glacial. Some area residents hold that its top third was built by hand.

moments.title: Lisbon
moments.text: The Scenic theater downtown has been showing pictures since 1911 and did not stop for 2020, when it moved the showings outdoors.
